content.text: {"persuasion":"UNPERSUADED","support_scope":"NONE","rationale":"The book establishes that bearing God’s name carries covenantal obligations, but it does not establish the stronger identity claim that the name is the covenant itself. The more economical interpretation is that a name represents its bearer’s identity, presence, honor, status, and authority; covenant belonging is one important consequence of bearing God’s name. This reading handles the temple, marriage, prayer, profanation, delegated authority, and reputation texts without converting every use into covenant language. Several crucial equations in the book—David’s ark with God’s name, a husband’s name with the marriage covenant itself, and Babel’s sought renown with a counterfeit covenant—are inferred rather than stated and are less natural than the counter-reading.","book_core_identification":"The name is the covenant itself: the binding relationship with God taken upon and owned by a person.","book_secondary_elaborations":["Taking the Lord’s name in vain primarily means claiming the covenant while living lawlessly, rather than merely misusing divine words.","Praying or acting in Jesus’ name means acting within the covenant and its terms.","A bride taking her husband’s name supplies the controlling model for bearing God’s name.","The husband’s wing or garment represents covenant covering, and its tasseled corners join the name to obedience to the commandments.","The temple, Davidic house, bridal covering, and preservation of a family name form one compounded symbolic structure.","The Lord’s Prayer is a miniature covenant renewal.","The names on the foreheads in Revelation represent opposing covenants owned by their bearers."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"A name represents and makes present the identity, standing, honor, and authority of its bearer. Being called by another’s name therefore signifies belonging to that person or house; acting in the name signifies claimed or delegated authority; honoring or profaning the name honors or dishonors the bearer. In covenantal settings these ideas naturally entail covenant membership and obligation, but the name does not denote the covenant itself.","counter_core_identification":"The name signifies the bearer’s identity, presence, status, honor, and authority; covenant belonging is a contextual implication rather than the name’s core referent.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The texts support a close association between God’s name and covenant membership, but not the book’s ontological equation, “the name is the covenant.” The bearer or the bearer’s recognized identity remains the more consistent referent.","counter_case":["In 2 Samuel 7:13, a house built “for my name” naturally means a sanctuary dedicated to God and representing his presence and honor. David’s preceding mention of the ark explains the temple context but does not make “name” lexically identical to “covenant.”","Isaiah 4:1 uses being “called by thy name” for recognized marital affiliation and removal of social reproach. That follows directly from taking the husband’s identity or household status; it does not require “name” to mean the marriage covenant itself.","Ruth 3:9 clearly depicts a marriage or redemption request through the spread garment, but the verse contains no name-language. Ezekiel 16 explicitly connects the same gesture with covenant, establishing garment or wing as covenantal covering—not establishing that “name” itself means covenant.","Exodus 20:7 is readily explained as falsely or emptily bearing, invoking, or using God’s identity and authority. Covenant hypocrisy is one serious instance, but the command’s name-language remains intelligible without replacing the bearer’s name with the covenant.","Matthew 7:22–23 distinguishes claimed use of Jesus’ name and authority from being known by him. This fits the common reading especially well: people can invoke or claim another’s authority falsely. The book must redefine their repeated “in thy name” claims as possession of only a sound.","Genesis 11:4 and 12:2 contrast humanly acquired renown with renown granted by God. Reputation or public identity explains “make us a name” directly, whereas calling Babel’s sought name a self-made covenant adds a concept not expressed in the passage.","The diverse constructions—building for a name, calling by a name, acting in a name, making a name great, and profaning a name—are naturally unified by reference to the bearer’s recognized identity and standing. The covenant equation needs a separate figurative bridge in each case."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["It compellingly emphasizes that bearing God’s name cannot be reduced to correct pronunciation or a verbal formula.","It gives a strong integrated account of covenant hypocrisy in Exodus 20:7, Ezekiel 36, Matthew 7, and the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer.","Its linkage of Isaiah 4, Ruth 3, and Ezekiel 16 illuminates the biblical association among marriage, belonging, covering, and covenant responsibility.","It explains why genuine appeal to God’s name should involve obedience and relationship rather than magical invocation."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["It preserves the ordinary semantic center of “name” while allowing covenant, marriage, authority, reputation, and presence to arise contextually.","It explains non-covenantal or only indirectly covenantal uses such as making a name, making a name great, and performing acts in another’s name without strained redefinition.","It distinguishes the person or identity represented by the name from the relationship that people enter with that person.","It does not depend on treating David’s mention of the ark and God’s later mention of the name as an explicit substitution or definition.","It explains false invocation in Matthew 7: people may claim Jesus’ identity and authority without possessing a genuine relationship with him.","It accommodates the book’s strongest ethical insights as implications of bearing God’s name rather than requiring them to define the symbol."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":["Genesis 11:4’s “let us make us a name” directly denotes renown or enduring corporate identity;
